keyVerseText: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S, and he hath set the world upon them.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun תֵּבֵל (têbêl) derives from the root יָבַל (yâbal), which means to bring forth, carry, or lead along, often with the sense of flowing or conducting. This root idea of movement and carrying suggests that תֵּבֵל originally conveyed the concept of the earth as a place that is brought forth or sustained, emphasizing its dynamic and life-supporting nature rather than a static object. This enriches the common English gloss 'world' by highlighting the earth as a habitable, flowing, and life-bearing domain.
usageInScripture: The word תֵּבֵל appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly translated as 'the world' or 'of the world,' indicating its broad usage to denote the habitable earth or the globe and its inhabitants. It is sometimes used poetically as a synonym for אֶרֶץ (erets, earth or land) and can refer specifically to certain lands like Babylonia or Palestine. The consistent translation as 'world' underscores its role in describing the totality of the inhabited earth and its peoples, reflecting a comprehensive view of God's creation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תֵּבֵל as the habitable, sustained world deepens our appreciation of God's sovereign rule over all creation. The earth is not merely a physical space but a divinely maintained realm where His purposes unfold. Recognizing the world as something 'borne' or 'carried' by God reminds believers of His providential care and authority. This word affirms that the entire inhabited earth belongs to the LORD, who upholds it and governs history, pointing us to Christ as the sovereign King over all the world He created and sustains.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Samuel 2:8 declares that God lifts the lowly and sets them among princes, affirming His power to exalt the humble. The verse concludes by stating that 'the pillars of the earth are the LORD’S, and he hath set the world upon them,' using תֵּבֵל to emphasize that the entire inhabited world rests securely on God's sovereign foundation. This portrays God not only as the moral ruler who raises the poor but also as the cosmic King who upholds the entire world, encouraging faith in His comprehensive dominion and care.
